title: Why Trump's H-1B Crackdown Could Be an 'Own Goal' for America
excerpt: The Times of India argues the $100,000 fee, fraud probes and green-card freezes will push innovation offshore — an industrial-policy gift to India disguised as worker protection.
body:
• In the Times of India's assessment, the Trump administration's H-1B crackdown — a one-time $100,000 fee on new petitions, fraud probes and green-card freezes — risks backfiring on the US economy while accelerating India's rise.
  • The columnist's core argument: when labor cannot move to capital, capital moves to labor — US firms will offshore work and expand Global Capability Centres in India instead of hiring Americans.
  • Indian industry voices echo the theme: former NITI Aayog CEO Amitabh Kant says the move will "choke US innovation and turbocharge India's," while Infosys veteran Mohandas Pai predicts an offshoring surge within a year.
  • What this means for you: the $100,000 fee is a one-time charge on new petitions only — existing H-1B holders, renewals and status changes are unaffected. Cap-exempt employers (universities, nonprofits, research labs) and higher-wage roles face less disruption, and India's GCC hiring boom gives skilled professionals a growing onshore alternative.

The Times of India has weighed the Trump administration's H-1B offensive — the $100,000 new-petition fee, the PERM suspensions of eight major employers, and a widening fraud probe — and rendered its verdict: an own goal. In the paper's analysis, a policy sold as protection for American workers will instead erode America's competitive edge, push jobs offshore, and hand India the very talent and investment Washington hoped to deny itself.

The columnist's logic is deliberately simple. The H-1B program exists because of a mismatch the administration's arithmetic ignores: American universities produce world-class talent, but not nearly enough engineers in the specialties tech firms need. Squeeze the legal channel and the work does not migrate to unemployed Americans — it migrates to Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Gurgaon. In TOI's framing, this is less immigration enforcement than an industrial policy that subsidizes India's Global Capability Centres.

The arguments for the "own goal"

First, the innovation drain. Former NITI Aayog CEO Amitabh Kant wrote on X that the fee would "choke US innovation, and turbocharge India's," arguing that "by slamming the door on global talent, America pushes the next wave of labs, patents, innovation and startups to Bangalore and Hyderabad, Pune and Gurgaon." His summary, as quoted by TOI: "America's loss will be India's gain."

Second, the offshoring accelerator. Infosys veteran and investor Mohandas Pai told PTI the fee was "regressive," predicting companies would respond within six months to a year by expanding offshore delivery rather than hiring locally. "Everybody will work to increase offshoring," he said, "because first, you don't get talent, second the costs are too high." Snapdeal co-founder Kunal Bahl made the human version of the same point, recalling his own H-1B rejection in 2007 while sitting at a Microsoft desk — "crushing and numbing at that moment, but life-changing eventually" — and telling today's affected workers that "something much bigger and better" awaits them in India.

Third, the domestic backlash. TOI notes the fee has drawn fire inside the US too: Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi called it "reckless," and Silicon Valley community leaders warned it would deter the top global talent that built the region's ecosystem. The paper points to the FY2025 H-1B approval table — Amazon at 10,044, TCS at 5,505, Microsoft at 5,189, Meta at 5,123, Apple at 4,202, Google at 4,181 — as evidence the fee taxes American champions as much as Indian outsourcing firms.

Where the administration's case stands

The column is candid that the administration's abuse claims are not invented: body-shopping, wage undercutting and sham job postings have dogged the program for years, and the Labor Department's fraud probe has found real back wages owed. TOI's counter is that the cure overshoots the disease — a flat $100,000 levy and blanket employer suspensions hit compliant sponsors alongside abusers, and the proposed wage-based lottery and narrowed exemptions would finish what the fee started.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian professionals, the paper's advice is implicit but clear: the American door is narrowing, but the Indian one is widening. With India's tech sector absorbing GCC investment and returning talent, TOI argues the diaspora's leverage has shifted — professionals who once accepted decade-long green-card queues now have credible onshore options, a dynamic the administration's math does not price in.

What's Next / Looking Ahead

The administration has extended the $100,000 fee regime through September 21, 2027, and a proposed rule replacing the random H-1B lottery with wage-weighted selection is still in the pipeline — changes TOI says would lock in the "own goal" for years. The real test, in the columnist's framing, is whether offshoring and GCC growth in India accelerate as predicted — or whether the crackdown actually rebuilds domestic hiring. Eighteen months of data will settle the argument.
